primary.description_medium: The supplied TrumpFile page points to the Supreme Court’s June 2014 Burwell v. Hobby Lobby decision. The opinion addressed claims by closely held for-profit corporations seeking relief from the federal contraceptive-coverage requirement under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. That is narrower than the page’s assertion that corporations generally have the same rights as natural persons. primary.description_long: The supplied TrumpFile entry concerns the Supreme Court’s June 30, 2014 decision in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. The opinion describes claims by owners of closely held for-profit corporations who objected on religious grounds to facilitating access to certain contraceptive drugs and devices through employee health coverage. The Court resolved a statutory claim under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. That case-specific ruling does not establish the entry’s sweeping suggestion that corporations generally hold the same rights as natural persons. The TrumpFile page itself makes that broader argument, but the packet identifies no Donald Trump statement, action, appointment, or role in the litigation or decision. This draft therefore preserves the identifiable legal subject while leaving the record’s Trump connection unresolved. It does not attribute the decision to Trump or present the dispute as an act of his administration. frozen_original.title: Trump Says He Will Not Accept 2028 Election Results If He Loses
frozen_original.synopsis: In September 2025, during interviews and rally appearances, Trump stated that he would not commit to accepting the results of the 2028 presidential election if he were to lose, continuing a pattern of preemptively refusing to commit to democratic transitions of power that he established before both the 2016 and 2020 elections. The statements alarmed democratic norms experts and drew condemnation from members of both parties. The refusal to commit to peaceful transfer of power was seen as particularly alarming given Trump's actions following the 2020 election and the January 6 Capitol attack. The statements also raised questions about Trump's intent regarding the 22nd Amendment and potential third-term ambitions.

frozen_original.title: DOGE Fires 1,300 Department of Education Employees
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency directed the termination of approximately 1,300 Department of Education employees — roughly half the department's total workforce — through a combination of mass firings and forced buyouts. Among those eliminated were staff overseeing Title I funding for low-income schools, special education enforcement under IDEA, student loan servicing oversight, and the Office for Civil Rights which investigated discrimination at schools. Education Secretary Linda McMahon described the firings as the first step toward eliminating the department entirely. States reported losing their primary federal contacts for education compliance. Civil rights complaints filed by students and parents began piling up with no staff to process them. Teachers unions called the action a deliberate sabotage of public education infrastructure.

primary.title: Education Department Announces Reduction Affecting 1,315 Employees
primary.description_short: On March 11, 2025, the Education Department announced a reduction affecting nearly half its workforce; ABC News reported notices to 1,315 employees.
primary.description_medium: On March 11, 2025, the Department of Education announced a reduction in force affecting nearly half its workforce. The department’s release said its total workforce would fall from 4,133 at inauguration to roughly 2,183 after the action. ABC News reported that notices went to 1,315 employees; affected staff were set to enter administrative leave on March 21. The accessed sources do not establish direct DOGE direction.
primary.description_long: The Department of Education announced a reduction in force on March 11, 2025. Its release said the action would affect nearly 50 percent of the department’s workforce and that impacted staff would be placed on administrative leave beginning March 21. The department listed 4,133 employees when President Trump took office and roughly 2,183 after the action; it said nearly 600 employees had already accepted voluntary resignation or retirement opportunities during the prior seven weeks. ABC News reported that reduction-in-force notices went to 1,315 employees on March 11 and that those affected were set to enter administrative leave on March 21, with pay and benefits through June 9. The department described the action as part of its “final mission.” This repaired account records the department’s announced workforce reduction and reported scale. The sources do not establish that DOGE directly ordered or carried out the reduction, so the frozen card’s DOGE attribution is omitted. The accessed sources also do not support the frozen card’s claims that particular program offices lost all staff, that compliance contacts disappeared, that complaints accumulated without staff, or that teachers unions called the action sabotage.

frozen_original.title: FBI under Patel investigates Trump's perceived enemies Milley Esper Romney
frozen_original.synopsis: Kash Patel's FBI opened investigations into Trump's political adversaries including General Mark Milley, former Defense Secretary Mark Esper, and Senator Mitt Romney, using federal law enforcement as an instrument of political vengeance. Milley and Esper had both publicly criticized Trump after leaving their positions, while Romney was one of the few Republican senators to vote against Trump in both impeachment trials. Former Justice Department officials called the investigations a return to the abuses of J. Edgar Hoover's era and a fundamental corruption of the FBI's mission.

primary.title: Unverified claim of FBI investigations into Milley, Esper and Romney
primary.description_short: The supplied record alleges April 2025 FBI investigations of Milley, Esper and Romney; its AP link gives background on Patel, not confirmation.
primary.description_medium: The frozen record alleges that FBI Director Kash Patel opened investigations in April 2025 into retired General Mark Milley, former Defense Secretary Mark Esper and Senator Mitt Romney as political adversaries. The packet gives no case records, agency statement or reporting confirming those investigations. Its Associated Press link describes Patel’s prior criticism of the FBI and support for Trump, but does not document inquiries into the three named people. This remains unverified.
primary.description_long: The frozen record alleges that, in April 2025, the FBI under Kash Patel opened investigations into Mark Milley, Mark Esper and Mitt Romney because they were perceived as political adversaries of Donald Trump. It says Milley and Esper had criticized Trump after leaving government and that Romney voted against Trump in both impeachment trials; the supplied packet provides no citations for the alleged investigations or their motive. Associated Press coverage dated January 30, 2025, characterized Patel as a staunch Trump defender and critic of the FBI while he was the nominee to lead the bureau. That background does not establish that he opened investigations into Milley, Esper or Romney, nor does it verify a shared target list or retaliatory purpose. Keep April 1 only as the supplied, unconfirmed start date. The alleged investigation, its subjects and the claim of political vengeance all require separate evidence before publication. This internal draft preserves the claim for review and does not represent it as a finding, charge, or confirmed FBI action.
primary.date_start_basis: Supplied original date; it is not independently verified as the start of an investigation.
